```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.5, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

Before any similarity measure is applied, a co-occurrence network rests on
a count: how much each transaction adds to the weight of each pair of its
items. The default, full counting, adds one for every pair in every
transaction. A transaction with \(n\) items therefore creates
\(n(n - 1)/2\) pairs, so a film with five genres contributes ten links and
a film with two genres one link, and transactions with many items dominate
the network. In bibliometrics this problem led to fractional counting, in
which each pair of a transaction with \(n\) items adds \(1/(n - 1)\), so
that the links of every item within one transaction sum to one
(Perianes-Rodriguez et al., 2016). For ordered transactions, such as
sessions of learning actions, a third option weights each pair by the
distance between the two items, so that items close together in a sequence
are linked more strongly than items far apart.

This guide compares the three methods available through the `counting`
argument of `cooccurrence()`. It shows what each method adds per
transaction, checks the weights by hand, and asks when the choice changes
the conclusions drawn from a network. Normalization of the counts by item
frequencies is a separate step, covered in
[Choosing a similarity measure](similarity-measures.html).

```{r package}
library(cooccure)
```

## Data

`movies` holds 1,000 highly rated IMDb films, one row per film:

- **Transaction:** the film (`tconst`).
- **Items:** `genres`, a comma-delimited string of one to three genres.

`actors` is a long table with one row per actor and film:

- **Items:** `actor`.
- **Transaction:** `tconst`, the film.

The number of items per transaction is what separates full from fractional
counting, so both distributions are shown first.

```{r transaction-sizes}
with(movies, table(n_genres = lengths(strsplit(genres, ","))))
with(actors, table(cast_size = table(tconst)))
```

Films carry one, two or three genres; 231 films have a single genre and add
nothing to the genre network under any counting method. Cast sizes in the
`actors` table vary far more, from 1 to 38 actors per film, because the
table keeps only actors who appear in at least two of the films.

## Full counting

Under full counting, each film adds one to each pair of its genres.

```{r full}
cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", top_n = 5)
```

*Comedy* and *Drama* share 159 films, so their weight is 159, equal to the
`count` column. Under full counting the weight and the count are always the
same.

## Fractional counting

Under fractional counting, a film with \(n\) genres adds \(1/(n - 1)\) to
each of its pairs: 1 for a two-genre film, 0.5 for a three-genre film.

```{r fractional}
cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",", counting = "fractional",
             top_n = 5)
```

The weight of *Comedy* and *Drama* falls from 159 to 107.5 while the count
stays at 159. The value can be checked from the composition of those 159
films.

```{r fractional-check}
with(movies, table(
  comedy_and_drama = grepl("Comedy", genres) & grepl("Drama", genres),
  n_genres = lengths(strsplit(genres, ","))
))
```

Of the 159 films, 56 carry two genres and add 1 each, and 103 carry three
genres and add 0.5 each: \(56 + 103 \times 0.5 = 107.5\).

Fractional counting has a second property that serves as a check: the
links of a genre within one film sum to one, so a genre's strength (the sum
of its edge weights) equals the number of its films that carry at least
one other genre.

```{r fractional-strength}
genre_fractional <- cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
                                 counting = "fractional")
head(as.data.frame(genre_fractional, what = "nodes"), 4)
with(movies, table(drama = grepl("Drama", genres),
                   several_genres = grepl(",", genres)))
```

*Drama* has a frequency of 634 films and a fractional strength of 504, the
number of *Drama* films with at least one other genre; the remaining 130
are tagged *Drama* alone. Under full counting the same strength is 812,
because three-genre films count twice for each of their genres.

## Does the counting method change the conclusions?

Because the films carry at most three genres, the two methods differ by at
most a factor of two per film, and the strongest raw pairs keep their order.
The difference grows once counts are normalized, because a measure such as
association strength divides by the item frequencies, which do not change
with the counting method.

```{r association-compare}
cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
             similarity = "association", top_n = 6)
cooccurrence(movies, field = "genres", sep = ",",
             similarity = "association", counting = "fractional", top_n = 6)
```

*History* and *News* lead under full counting (0.01613) but drop to second
under fractional counting (0.00806). The ratio of 0.5 shows that their one
shared film carries three genres. *Horror* and *Sci-Fi* keep three quarters
of their weight (0.01136 to 0.00852), since one of their two shared films
has two genres and the other three, and they move to the top. *Documentary*
and *Music* enter the six strongest pairs under fractional counting. The
ranking of pairs that rest on one or two films is fragile under both
methods, which is a reason to combine association strength with
`min_occur`.

## Casts of different sizes

The case for fractional counting is stronger when transaction sizes vary
widely, as the casts in `actors` do. Under full counting, an actor in a
38-member cast gains 37 links from that one film.

```{r actors-full}
actors_full <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst")
actors_fractional <- cooccurrence(actors, field = "actor", by = "tconst",
                                  counting = "fractional")
subset(as.data.frame(actors_full, what = "nodes"),
       node %in% c("Brad Rea", "Julia Bache-Wiig"))
subset(as.data.frame(actors_fractional, what = "nodes"),
       node %in% c("Brad Rea", "Julia Bache-Wiig"))
```

Brad Rea appears in two films with large casts in the table and reaches a
degree of 66 and a full-counting strength of 70. Julia Bache-Wiig appears in three films with small casts and has a
strength of 7. Under fractional counting their strengths become 2 and 3:
one per film with at least one co-star in the table. Fractional counting
thus ranks actors by the number of collaborative films rather than by the
size of their casts. Degree, a count of distinct co-stars, does not change
with the counting method.

```{r actors-pair}
subset(as.data.frame(actors_fractional), from == "Julia Bache-Wiig")
```

The pair Julia Bache-Wiig and Robin Ottersen shares three films (count 3)
but keeps a fractional weight of 1.33, because the casts of some of those
films include further actors of the table.

## Attention counting for ordered transactions

When the items of a transaction are ordered, such as the states of a
learning session, full and fractional counting ignore the order. Attention
counting adds \(\exp(-|p_i - p_j| / \lambda)\) for each pair, where
\(p_i\) and \(p_j\) are the positions of the two items, so the
contribution decays with their distance. A single sequence of three states
shows the weights.

```{r attention-hand}
cooccurrence(list(c("A", "B", "C")), counting = "attention")
```

Adjacent states add \(e^{-1} = 0.368\) and states two positions apart add
\(e^{-2} = 0.135\), while the `count` column still records one shared
transaction. Repeated states are removed before positions are assigned, so
each state keeps the position of its first occurrence.

The bundled data are not ordered, so the six learning sessions of the
[sequences guide](sequences.html) illustrate the method.

```{r sessions}
sessions <- data.frame(
  t1 = c("plan",    "plan",   "read",   "plan",    "read",    "plan"),
  t2 = c("read",    "read",   "write",  "read",    "read",    "write"),
  t3 = c("write",   "read",   "review", "discuss", "write",   "review"),
  t4 = c("review",  "write",  "write",  "write",   "discuss", "write"),
  t5 = c("write",   "review", NA,       "review",  "write",   "review"),
  t6 = c("discuss", NA,       NA,       "plan",    "review",  NA)
)
cooccurrence(sessions, field = "all", counting = "attention")
```

Under full counting, *read* and *review* share five sessions, the second
highest count (see the [sequences guide](sequences.html)). Under attention counting
they fall to a weight of 0.506, below *plan* and *read* (1.104), which
share only three sessions but always as neighbors. The decay rate
`lambda` sets how fast distance is penalized.

```{r attention-lambda}
cooccurrence(sessions, field = "all", counting = "attention", lambda = 3)
```

With `lambda = 3`, distant pairs keep more of their weight and *read* and
*review* return to third place (2.276). As `lambda` grows, attention
counting approaches full counting; as it shrinks, only adjacent states
contribute. Attention counting can also be combined with `window`, so that
pairs beyond the window contribute nothing and pairs within it are
weighted by distance.

## Counting with weighted input

A long table with a weight column (`weight_by`) already defines how much
each item contributes to its transaction, as described in
[Input formats](input-formats.html). Fractional and attention counting
derive that contribution from the number or the positions of the items, so
the two cannot be combined: `cooccurrence()` raises an error of class
`cooccure_incompatible_args` when `weight_by` is given with a counting
method other than `"full"`.

## References

Perianes-Rodriguez, A., Waltman, L., & van Eck, N. J. (2016). Constructing
bibliometric networks: A comparison between full and fractional counting.
*Journal of Informetrics*, *10*(4), 1178--1195.
<https://doi.org/10.1016/j.joi.2016.10.006>
